title: Cove OR Crown...room by room | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bjstem", "author_name": "bjstem", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bjstem", "date": "2025-01-01", "text": "Hello detail people! Happy New Year! I wanted to run something by some of you.  I'm looking at an issue that I didn't see on paper, and now it looks hinky in execution and I'm thinking of another solution. The living room and foyer have higher ceilings, and I went with 4.5\" crown mouldings, but now I'm looking at the Kitchen and Master, and I'm wondering if the 3.5\" cove moulding instead of crown, is going to give a cleaner, airier look for those rooms.  (None of it is stained -- it's all painted mouldings.) Is it necessary to keep one moulding style consistently throughout the entire house? I'm actually thinking of shifting to a slimmer (3.5\") cove profile for the walkout basement level, as well, to have a more modern look than was originally the plan.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~125880644", "author_name": "Diana Bier Interiors, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~125880644", "date": "2025-01-02", "text": "Style and size are two different factors.  You should keep to a similar style and level of formality in the house.  So any of the classical styles of crown molding would work in a home that calls for that--a Colonial revival, Tudor, Italianate, Queen Anne, Greek Revival, and the like. title: Benefits of a Folding Treadmill with Incline | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "relife-sports-pfvwus-pf~944447487", "author_name": "Relife sports", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/home-stagers/relife-sports-pfvwus-pf~944447487", "date": "2025-01-02", "text": "A folding treadmill with incline combines the convenience of a space-saving, foldable design with the added challenge of an incline feature, which helps enhance your workout by targeting different muscle groups and increasing calorie burn. These treadmills are perfect for home use, offering an effective cardiovascular workout while allowing you to easily store the machine when not in use. Key Features of Folding Treadmill with Incline Incline Functionality Manual vs. Motorized: Some folding treadmills offer manual incline, where you have to adjust the incline manually by shifting the deck, while others provide motorized incline that adjusts automatically with the push of a button. Motorized inclines are more convenient, but manual inclines often come at a lower price. Range of Incline: The incline range typically varies from 0% to 10\u201320%. A higher incline percentage provides a steeper slope for a more challenging workout. Folding Mechanism The key advantage of a folding treadmill with Incline is its ability to save space when not in use. Most folding models feature a hydraulic or soft-drop folding system for easy and safe folding. Some also come with a vertical fold where the running deck folds upright, and others have a horizontal fold. Running Surface Belt Size: A larger running belt (typically 50\u201360 inches long and 18\u201322 inches wide) offers more comfort, especially for taller or longer strides. Make sure the surface is sufficient for your needs. Cushioning: Many folding treadmills come with shock absorption systems that reduce the impact on joints, making them gentler on your knees, hips, and back. Speed and Motor Power Look for a treadmill with a motorized motor that offers speeds ranging from 0.5 to 12 mph (1\u201319 km/h). A motor with 2.0\u20133.5 HP is typical for home treadmills and provides enough power for jogging or running, especially with the incline feature. Build Quality Frame Construction: A sturdy metal frame ensures stability, especially when walking or running at higher speeds or steeper inclines. Weight Capacity: The typical weight capacity ranges from 220 to 350 lbs (100\u2013159 kg). Ensure the treadmill can support your weight, especially if you plan to use it regularly. Console and Features Display: Look for a console with a clear display showing essential workout stats like speed, incline, time, distance, calories burned, and heart rate. Workout Programs: Many folding treadmills come with preset workout programs that automatically adjust speed and incline. Programs may target fat-burning, interval training, or cardio fitness. Connectivity: Some modern treadmills have Bluetooth compatibility, smartphone apps, or USB ports for entertainment or tracking your progress with fitness apps. Benefits of a Folding Treadmill with Incline Space Saving: The ability to fold the treadmill makes it ideal for home use, especially in apartments or rooms with limited space. Varied Workouts: The incline feature provides the ability to perform hill climbs, which can help increase calorie burn, target different muscle groups (especially the glutes and calves), and improve cardiovascular endurance. Convenience: The foldable design allows for easy storage and use, and many models feature wheels for easy transport. Customizable Intensity: The combination of adjustable speeds and inclines provides an effective way to vary the intensity of your workouts. You can perform moderate walks with a slight incline or intense interval training with a steeper incline. A folding treadmill with incline is a great option for anyone looking for a versatile and space-efficient home cardio machine. When choosing one, ensure it meets your specific needs, such as a motorized or manual incline, suitable speed range, and adequate running surface.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kandrewspa", "author_name": "kandrewspa", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kandrewspa", "date": "2025-01-04", "text": "I think any white is going to be too white against the wood trim and fireplace stone.  Get a bunch of off white chips from whichever manufacturer you prefer and focus on finding a color that works with the kitchen counter, wood elements and fireplace.  If you prefer BM, look at Navajo White like another commenter suggested as this is a tried and true for going with warm woodwork.  Also Edgecomb Gray if you like a darker color.  It's not very gray so it would be an update without being tremendously different than what you have.  It's very popular as it's very versatile.  Also look at Ballet White and Winds Breath. Sampling is so important, especially when you're going to paint a large area and maybe pay someone to do it since you have high ceilings.  DH bought a standard sized piece of drywall, cut it into four pieces and we sampled colors on it to get a good idea of what colors would look like.  Paint chips are too small, although they're a good starting point.  Samplize samples, which are about the size of a piece a paper, are a good intermediate step. Some rooms are more difficult than others to find the right color for.  Sometimes I hit it on the first try, others I have had to try ten different colors for, and the average is 3-5. title: Kitchen advice - British, German or Italian brands? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "baljeet-nijjhar", "author_name": "B N", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/baljeet-nijjhar", "date": "2025-01-04", "text": "So I've been doing lots of research on these. I'm after the handleless style with the handleless rail, not the J-pull. I also like the idea of a lower plinth and taller floor units i.e. 10 cm plinth and 78 cm floor units, not the 15 cm / 720 cm standard that the main British manufacturers do. I also feel (rightly or wrongly) that those kitchen manufacturers that supply backboards which are 3 mm (Hacker, Leicht to name a couple) are indicative of not being as good quality overall as those which are 8 or 10 mm. This has led me to look into German and Italian brands such as Rempp, Ballerina, Rotpunkt, KH System Mobel, Stosa, Pedini, Modulnova etc. I can see that the Italian doors tend to be thicker and weightier than German ones (I have heard that in Germany, it's common to take your kitchen with you when you rent, so maybe they are lighter?) But I can't for the life of me work out whether Italian manufacturers use materials to make their cabinets which make them longer lasting than German ones. Do they use better quality materials like green chipboard / plywood / higher density chipboard? I don't want to spend \u00a340K on a kitchen overall and not have a robust, stylish kitchen for years to come. So I'm asking kitchen fitters out there what they've seen when they have come to fit them - which brands seem great quality and have lasted well in your view and why? And is there an actual British brand that does handleless and low plinth, or is it only bespoke kitchens where I might find this?", "images": []}

title: step-in v. wheel-in showers? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "izzbudcan23", "author_name": "izzbudcan23", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/izzbudcan23", "date": "2025-01-05", "text": "hi, all - what are some high-level thoughts on step-in v wheel-in showers?  thinking ahead, if we do a no-sill shower to enable future \"elder\" access, do we need to do a full wet room treatment?  if we start off w glass wall/door combo (could be removed later for a curtain option), does that only work on a shower w a sill?  our . bathroom is on the compact side but already has an older kohler steam shower, so that alcove is oversized and would convert well to a regular shower -just trying to decide on type.  thanks!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "tlbp514", "author_name": "Mrs Pete", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tlbp514", "date": "2025-01-06", "text": "Random thoughts on step-in vs. wheel-in: - If you're in a wheelchair now, or if you have a debilitating condition that might suggest future need, consider the wheel-in options.  If you don't fit that profile, your chances of being permanently in a wheelchair (due to normal aging) is about 4%.  That's pretty low -- and if you were in that 4%, you'd probably need to move anyway. - Someone will say, \"Better to have it ...\"  Yeah, I see that line of reasoning, but roll-in showers are more expensive to build, require more space, and (because they're harder to install and fewer people have experience with them) they more often spill water out onto the bathroom floor.  Don't spend more and risk trouble for a low-possibility event, especially when other options exist. - Consider that step-ins aren't all the same.  My bedroom shower curb (from the 1970s) is something like 6\" high, and I stub my toe on it fairly often -- hate that thing.  A minimum curb is only 2\" -- we went with that when we replaced our hall shower, and it's a whole different ballgame -- a wheelchair can roll over 2\", especially with help entering /exiting the shower.  Consider, too, that shower curbs can be very narrow or rather wide -- and that can make a difference in stepping over. - Consider a slide-in bench.  These are wide benches that allow you to sit down, then \"slide over\" into the tub /no curb concerns. - Or consider the most simple of all options:  A simple hospital shower chair; most wheelchair users can walk a few steps (especially if you're talking about normal aging and not trauma or neurological issues) and get into the chair. - Do not build in a bench -- if you want seating now, go with a teak stool.  A built-in bench could remove the possibility of using these simple add-ons later. - No to a full wet room.  That's overkill. Other thoughts about making a shower elder-friendly: - Definitely place your grab bars now.  Adding them later will almost certainly penetrate your waterproofing barrier and cause mold behind your tiles. - Ideally you'd have a vertical bar just outside the shower /another just inside the shower to assist with entry /exit.  And you'd have a horizontal bar across the back side of the shower.  And you'd have a vertical bar next to the shower head so you can hold onto it while reaching for the shower head. - Note that grab bars \"cut into\" your shower's size -- so go a bit larger than you think you actually need. - Instead of the expected glass door, go with a shower curtain.  It's easier to keep clean now, and -- if you need it in the future -- it'll allow you wider access to the shower. - Go with a floor-to-ceiling curtain (perhaps custom-made), and it'll look better than a glass door too. - Definitely go with a hand-held shower head.  (No need for a standard shower head in addition.)  Consider one on a sliding rail, which will allow you to easily use it from a standing or sitting position.  Be sure, too, that the shower head can reach the farthest corner of the shower enclosure for easy cleaning. - Position your on /off switches so you can reach in and turn the water on without entering the shower /without committing your body to the initial cold spray. - Place your shower niche (or other storage) low enough that it'll be useful from a sitting position. - Position your towel bars so that you can easily reach them from the shower. - Consider a Tornado Body Dryer and eliminate the need for towels. - Consider that if you need a walker or wheelchair, you may need to get rid of throw rugs, which are trip hazards.  As my grandmother neared 100, her #1 problem wasn't getting through doorways or entering the shower -- it was those nasty thresholds and changes in flooring and throw rugs, which would make her fall /throw her to the floor.  If you think loss of your bath mat will really bother you, consider building in heated flooring. - Everyone on this board seems to consider tile a necessity.  Consider linoleum instead.  It's softer underfoot and will be kinder to your ankles and knees as you age, and -- if you do fall -- it's softer /less likely to lead to a broken bone.  It's also warmer underfoot.", "images": []}}

Im Treppenhaus w\u00fcrden wir jeweils auf halber H\u00f6he der Stufen eine Wandlampe vorsehen, die mit der Deckenlampe vom Flur DG bzw. Flur UG geschaltet wird. Bei Verwendung der dicken Bretter (identisch mit den Stufen) reicht eine Fixierung an der Stufe und eine weitere an der Wand gegen\u00fcber. Da wird sicher nichts durchbiegen. Maximal zur Sicherheit einen kleinen Wandwinkel mittig zur Fixierung. Wichtig, da\u00df der erste Boden mit einer Sockelblende bis zum Boden (!) in gleichem Material geschlossen wird. Er sollte ein \"Podest\" bilden, da\u00df keinen Platz zum Drunterschieben bietet. Die Kisten solten bewusst NICHT mehr auf dem Boden (also irgendwo im Raum) abgestellt werden, sondern bewusst \"im Setzkasten\" stehen. . Und KEINE Transparenten Kisten verwenden. Es ist bei Lagerraum zwar f\u00fcr die innere Ruhe wichtig, den Inhalt zu kennen, aber das geht mit Einsteckschildern viel wohnlicher. Auch keine seltsamen Formate aussuchen. Am besten Kisten mit geraden W\u00e4nden. Es gibt in Baum\u00e4rkten einfache Holzkisten, die sich hervorragend eignen w\u00fcrden. An diese Kisten einfach eine Einsteckschild schrauben, und schon kann man auch Jahre nach dem Einsortieren dort einfach ablesen, was man damals versenkt hatte. Einfacher wird es auch, wenn man ALLE Pl\u00e4tze mit den gleichen Kisten ausgestattet hat, und sich selbst verbietet, irgendwelche anderen Kartons etc. dort zu stapeln. \"Keinbe Ausnahmen\" ist eine einfache Regel, die man sich gut auferlegen kann. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "originalbestyears", "author_name": "Bestyears", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/originalbestyears", "date": "2025-01-07", "text": "I've been sewing for more than 40 years. Most of the fancy stitches and features of any machine will go unused.and I use the straight stitch, the zigzag, a stretch stitch, my buttonhole maker, and that's about it. The real test for a sewing machine is the quality of its straight stitch: Will the machine consistently stitch a straight, even line of stitche that looks nice on both the top and the bottom? The most common problems with so many machines are: the tension goes off, the bobbin tangles easily, the bobbins don't wind consistently well, etc. It can be frustrating, particularly for new sewists, who don't know how to troubleshoot. My best advice is to go to a sewing machine shop in your town or nearby, and ask them to see used machines. A $300 used machine from them will be a consistently better machine than the bells and whistles machines you can buy new. And equally important: most of these shops throw in free lessons, \"Getting Started With Sewing/Getting to Know Your Machine,\" type of thing. I guarantee, your daughter will learns tips and tricks in this class that she will call upon all of her sewing life. There is a website called Pattern Review where you can read machine reviews too. main_question: {"author_id": "cherryfizz", "author_name": "Cherryfizz", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cherryfizz", "date": "2025-01-07", "text": "The day after Christmas I woke up with severe, worse pain I have ever felt in my left hip and shoulder. I must have turned funny in bed but when I got up I could hardly walk. My cousin told me to call an Ambulance but I told her not to be ridiculous, the pain should eventually subside but believe me it only got worse. Finally at 8 pm I had to make the call. I had an x-ray, blood tests taken, given Tylenol for the pain. The Doctor thought maybe I had a tissue tear.  After having a CT scan and waiting to see what they were going to do next 2 Doctors came over to talk to me. They asked me if I had fallen out of bed and I said no, I just turned funny during my 3 hours of sleep and woke up in pain.  The woman Doctor said they found a protein enzyme in my blood that \"pissed off\" my heart and said I may have had a blood clot or heart attack.  While I was waiting in triage I did experience chest pain but didn't mention it because I thought it was related to the pain I was already in. I  was admitted and sent to another area where I was taken care of, the nurse would not let me do anything on my own. My heart was monitored. They wanted to give me morphine but I said I didn't want any narcotics. I had an ekg and more blood taken.  We have 2 hospitals here and the one I was  in is more for trauma, respiratory and the other takes care of heart patients so the nurse said I was going for a ride and I was transferred to the Critical Cardiac Care floor. I was brought into a private room, thankfully with a window that opened hooked up to monitors, another blood test and a heart ultrasound.  With their help I was able to get up to use the washroom but my wires only reached that far. My Goal Board said Rest, Manage Pain, Morning Labs, Morning EKG, Daily Weigh In and being poked and prodded and blood pressure taken every few hours. I was given 2 types of blood thinners, one was an injection to the stomach, Tylenol 3, diuretics, and a Statin which I was not happy about taking. The Doctor came in the 2nd day I was there. I asked if they knew anything yet if I had a blood clot or heart attack and they were still investigating and he wanted me to have an Angiogram which scared me to have. He said after that they would know but for now just get rest. I was sent down for the Angiogram on Tuesday.  I was pretty calm, letting the nurse do what he had to do. The Doctor doing the Angiogram came over to talk to me and was very calming. They were going to do the test through my wrist rather than my groin which is less painful. I was brought into the room and was talking to the nurse one minute and the next minute the Doctor was calling my name and said they did not find any blockages. I was so happy to hear that because I have been on a higher fat diet. Just as they were wheeling me out of the room I started throwing up and my bowels let loose because of the twilight sedation. How embarrassing, you lose all dignity having to have someone clean you up. I hadn't thrown up in 20 or more years.  I was sick again back in my room and the next day so the Nurse told the Doctor he wanted to keep me in. The next morning the Dietician came in and said she wanted to talk about a Heart Healthy Diet and asked me what I thought that was.  My Goal Board said my food in the hospital was low fat and low sodium.  I told her my idea of a heart healthy diet would be different than hers after the hundreds of hours of research I have done the last 2 years. I said low fat has caused the obesity and diabetic epidemic. I told her that Ansel Keys who recommended to the government that people should be eating low fat after one of your Presidents had a heart attack so that is what went on the Food Pyramid but now that research has been debunked, he was wrong, and even his family is making public his research papers that shows his research was wrong.  I said eating fat is not your enemy, it is actually good for the heart, even saturated fat. I told her I eat cheese, butter, bacon, tallow for cooking, lots of eggs, some vegetables and fruit, chicken, fish, pork and red meat, no grains, pasta, starchy vegetables, no bread. I eat moderate fat that is mostly in the food.  After losing 100 pounds I allow myself up to 50 whole carbs a day from 20 so I can have more salad vegetables. The Doctor I follow and have taken his classes is a world renowned Keto Diet and Obesity Specialist and an Internist and has a clinic at Duke University. The Dietician handed me some papers and on the papers were my blood test results. My A1C is low, my Triglycerides are 0.70 below the Target of less than 1.7. LDL Cholesterol is 1.36 below the Target of less than 2.0. HDL Cholesterol is 1.32 the Target being Greater than 1.0. Total Cholesterol/HDL Ratio is 3.0, the Target is Less than 4.0.  Surprising me the Dietician said whatever you are eating is heart healthy and is working for you and to just keep on doing it and she left the room.  I am sure eating the way I do is not for everyone and low fat for them is the way to go and whatever works for you is what you should do to keep your levels below the Targets. The Doctor came in on Thursday and said I could go home, I have follow up appointments with my Cardiologist for another ultrasound and EKGs and he will tell me why they thought I had a heart attack or blood clot which I really think I did not have. I must say I had the best health care, the nursing staff and technicians were wonderful,   all so kind and really took care of me. I couldn't have had a better group of nursing staff taking care of me and we had lots of laughs. They loved coming into my room because I had the window wide open all day and night and they came in to cool off because it was so hot in the hospital. I am going to bring them a bunch of Tim Horton's gift cards because there is a Timmies in the lobby and a grocery card to the nearby walking distance to the store to get food or snacks.  I am so appreciative of their care.  It is good to be home I have to say the first 2 days I was in both hospitals I brought lots of smiles to peoples faces and that made me happy because of where they were. even all the EMTs waiting with their patients. When I was brought into the hospital I was wearing Grinch pajamas.  As I was wheeled up and down the halls everyone commented and said how much they loved I was wearing them and they all had big smiles on their faces.  It was nice though to change into fresh pjs that my cousin brought in for me.  Sorry this was so long.", "images": []}

title: the fallacy of plant wrapping for frost protection | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2025-01-07", "text": "Every winter, when we get a freeze, I see people who have carefully wrapped their plants in plastic or cloth. That DOES NOT PROTECT FROM THE COLD. The temperature inside a ball of plastic or cloth is the same outside the ball. What protects plants is to include soil in the wrap. That is, make a tent over the plant that contains the ground at the base. It's the soil that contributes heat, and keeps the temperature in the tent above the outside air temperature. That being said, if you're moist, wind chill can lower the temperature below the ambient temperature, but WIND CHILL DOES NOT AFFECT PLANTS. Wind with dry air can dry out plants, but that's a different matter. I will add that with a transparent covering, in the daytime, sunlight can heat up the interior somewhat, but the real threat is at night, when there is no such heat source.", "images": []}

It's all the way to ceiling, so it's like a full wall. I think it works well. One problem will be how to light the ref block, pantry cabs, and nook table from the vault. OP's often ask specific questions, and the commentariat brings up other stuff. Sometimes OPs get offended by that, I hope you don't. There a couple things I see that bring up a few questions: - The drawings are not correct, both the architect's and yours. Sometimes that doesn't matter, but it seems here you have some clearance conflicts where it does. You have some as-built dimensions now thinking about circulation clearances, but you need a full as-built of the space as it stands now. It should be drawn correctly and with the kitchen plan inserted. That would be helpful in seeing how say, the stair wall aligns with the nook window and if it interferes with the table seating, what dimension the hearth extension can be (will circulation have to cross over it), or where the existing hallway/beam aligns with all this (your last drawing shows a pocket door to the bathroom and impossible dimensions for a hallway). Field adjustments to design are a normal occurrence, and some parts of your design impinges on what exists in reality which is different than what was shown on paper. - There might be a concern with how your contractor made these alterations. Your former truss system had the \"ceiling\" bottom chord which kept your walls from pushing out. When you choose the alternate structural framing method of a ridge beam, that takes the place of the \"ceiling\" tying your walls together to keep them upright. However, the trusses were demo'd without the ridge beam installed, and no shoring was put under the old trusses/newLVLs as they went along removing each truss. I see you have snow currently on the roof, and no matter how little, there is a load + dynamic load on the roof. What can happen, and immediately, is because there is no ridge beam, the ridge of the rafters will sag, and simultaneously the top of walls will push out. This can be just 1/2\", but that can wreck a lot of plans. The contractor must verify the plumbness of the rafter heel walls and run a laser to check for sag at the ridge. - The other structural concern is in regards to the gable end wall. Before when you had trusses, the entire truss system including the gable ends worked as a diaphragm to brace against lateral loads. So the gable wall was split at the top plate (at about 8') which matched the truss ceiling. This all worked as it should. However, now that the trusses are removed (the remaining \"soffit\" truss has no structural value for lateral loads), your gable wall still has that top plate (at about 8') break in the wall, which acts as a hinge point. Winds and roof loads will cause the wall to \"fold\" at that top plate. Again, it may be only 1/2\" but over time with high winds can wreck a house. The contractor will eventually have to install the post in the wall for the ridge beam, but you also need full height studs (balloon framing) going from floor to top of gable wall uninterrupted to eliminate the hinge. These studs might only need to be say every 48\"o.c., it would be based on your Montana wind loads.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kendrahhendra", "author_name": "Kendrah", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kendrahhendra", "date": "2025-01-08", "text": "I've redone 2 of my own NYC coop kitchens now.  You are going to have a hard time getting quality work done for $15-20k max.   I have neighbors who did renovations for around that, and they loved their kitchens, but the quality sucked.  I mean 6 months later and things are falling off of the wall kind of sucked and the use of space was horrific. How long have you lived in this apartment and how badly do you need a kitchen renovation?  One thought is to make a few temporary improvements while you save a few years to be able to afford more quality renovation.  I'm still talking about getting an Ikea kitchen in a few years, but a well done job. For now, for $1,000 you could put down a nicer looking linoleum floor.  Paint the walls and ceiling. Get a new light fixture and faucet.  Add a few free standing storage pieces to the empty wall.  And make it aesthetically more appealing.  This will hold you over for a few years. If you do end up renovating, here is what I have learned to keep the costs down in a coop renovation: - Read your house rules.  Know what kinds of contractors you can and cannot use, what kinds of fees you might have to pay to do work in the building, to reserve the use of elevators, to have the plumbing shut off for work if needed - that kind of thing.  Depending on your rules it can add to your total budget. - Don't move the location of any plumbing, gas, or electric.  At all.  Like not even a few inches. - Know what your walls are made out of, where there are concrete columns and concrete beams. - Don't add extra j-boxes or recessed lights to the ceiling if your ceiling is plaster. - Life is easier if you have worked with contractors who know where to park in your neighborhood and who have worked in your building.  (Some may charge you if they get lots of tickets or if they have to pay to grease the palms of the maintenance workers in your building.) - Understand where demo debris gets taken to and what costs are involved. Most folks on Houzz do not live in the city.  Most costs they give you as estimates do not account for the insane cost of labor here, doing work in an old apartment building where removing walls is costly and often involves permission, working in an apartment where walls are uneven, walls are plaster, things are not easily hung, and contractors will sometimes give you beef about using Ikea cabinets.  (They don't want to sit and fiddle with putting together Ikea cabinets.  They'd rather sell you their own cabinets because everybody's gotta guy who can get you cabinet for less. title: Key Features to Look for in a Walking Treadmill with Incline | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "relife-sports-pfvwus-pf~944447487", "author_name": "Relife sports", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/home-stagers/relife-sports-pfvwus-pf~944447487", "date": "2025-01-11", "text": "A walking treadmill with an incline is an excellent choice for those looking to intensify their walking workouts, target different muscle groups, and improve cardiovascular health. The incline feature simulates uphill walking, which increases the intensity of your workout without needing to run or jog. Benefits of a Treadmill with Incline Increased Calorie Burn: Walking on an incline engages more muscles, leading to higher calorie expenditure compared to walking on a flat surface. Muscle Toning: An incline targets the calves, glutes, hamstrings, and quads, helping tone and strengthen the lower body. Cardiovascular Improvements: Uphill walking can improve heart health, as it increases the heart rate and enhances cardiovascular endurance. Reduced Impact: Walking on an incline is easier on the joints compared to running, making it a good option for those with joint concerns. Varied Workouts: The ability to adjust the incline allows for varied workouts, which can help avoid workout plateaus and keep things interesting. Key Features to Look for in a Walking Treadmill with Incline Incline Range: Most walking treadmills with incline offer adjustable inclines from 0% to 10-15%. Higher-end models may offer even steeper inclines, which can simulate walking up very steep hills. Motor Power: A motor between 1.5 HP and 2.5 HP is sufficient for walking with incline. A more powerful motor ensures smoother operation and supports longer workout sessions. Incline Adjustment Mechanism: Some treadmills allow manual incline adjustment, while others feature automatic incline adjustments that can be changed at the touch of a button. Automatic adjustments are more convenient during workouts, as they allow you to change the incline without stopping. Speed Range: Most walking treadmills with incline offer a speed range from 0.5 mph to 5 mph, which is adequate for walking workouts. Some models may go higher for brisk walking or light jogging. Walking Surface: Ensure the walking belt is long and wide enough for your stride. A standard length for walking is around 50-55 inches, with a width of 18-20 inches. Cushioning: Look for a treadmill with cushioning to reduce impact on your joints. This is especially important for incline walking, as the added slope can increase strain on the knees and ankles. Size and Storage: Many incline models are designed to fold for easier storage when not in use. Console and Programs: Many treadmills with incline come with preset workout programs, including hill and incline-specific routines. Some models also have heart rate monitors, Bluetooth connectivity, and other smart features for tracking your workouts. Things to Keep in Mind Weight Capacity: Ensure the treadmill has a weight capacity that supports your needs. Most incline treadmills can handle 250-350 lbs. Noise Level: Treadmills with incline can be louder during use, especially when the incline is adjusted. Consider models with noise-reducing features if noise is a concern. Warranty: Look for models with good warranties, especially for the motor and frame. This ensures long-term durability. A walking treadmill with incline can enhance your fitness routine, providing a more challenging and effective workout. It's a great way to boost endurance, burn more calories, and target specific muscle groups while being gentle on the joints. Whether for casual walking or a more intense workout, an incline treadmill is a versatile addition to your home gym.", "images": []}

title: Leak behind shower wall -- shear wall -- diagnosis & how to fix? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "coastal-vibe", "author_name": "coastal_vibe", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/coastal-vibe", "date": "2025-01-14", "text": "The 1st floor shower has a slow leak into the drywall next to the shower compartment. Cutting into the damaged drywall (next to the bottom corner of the shower), reveals a slow drip inside the wall (behind the tile), only when the shower is running. I am in CA -- the waterproofing (hot mop) for the shower pan is in tact -- passed the flood test. The plumber who looked at it last week is advertised as a \"leak detection\" company. He hesitated to check the shower valves and connections from behind the shower because it is a shear wall (interior wall). He suggested that it must be a problem with the waterproofing of the shower walls. I am convinced that it is a plumbing problem that can be fixed without ripping out the shower tiles and rebuilding. I called another plumber who may be able to look at it in a couple weeks. My question is about the shear wall issue. Will a big chunk of the shear wall need to be cut to access the plumbing?  Can plumbing be repaired from the tiled side of the shower without compromising the waterproofing in the walls? I took photos (attached) of the plumbing installation before the walls were closed. The pipes are copper \"L\" -- plumbing valves (thermostatic, volume, and 2-way diverter) are Kallista (Kohler).", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/eb72ad620785cc1f_1795-w500-h581-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2025-01-31", "text": "So, what you know is that it's not the plumbing. I suspect the shower curb also tilts out - and that the connection to the glass (or the door there) isn't water tight and the water is getting to the outside corner of the shower. I want gas. I'd be happy with four burners, but they all seem to have five. That's okay, but I have no use for a long oval burner in the middle, and with my nice collection of cast-iron cookward, I have no use for one of the ubiquitous long, skinny griddles. I don't want \"smart.\" I'm not attached to my  phone. I'm lucky if I know where it is. I'm a fan of Alexa, but I'm sure I can manage a new stove without her help. I have a small air fryer; I don't need my new oven to become a giant one. I do want convection, and that's close to the same thing. I went to the local appliance store where I got my freezer and dishwasher; the salesman is new to me.  It's clear that he thinks I can't afford very much. He's mentioned my \"budget\" more than once (his word, not mine) and  tried to steer me to low-end models. It's been bitter cold here, and I always arrive bundled up, so maybe that's how he got this impression. Or maybe it's my age. Or my very dirty car. (It's that time of year.) I've never encountered this before, and it's beginning to get irritating. When I told him which refrigerator I wanted (not high-end by a long shot, but in the $2,000 range) he challenged me on it, producing numbers he had worked up to show how much I'd save by getting a less expensive model. Maybe he needs to get that model off the floor. I don't know. But my current appliances are 23 years old, so I've had a long time to save for this purchase. \ud83d\ude0a Anyway, I thought I'd found the perfect gas range for me: a KitchenAid KFGG500ESS. Five burners, yes, but the one in the middle is small and round. Not \"smart.\" True convection. Nice looking. Decent brand. I was excited! But then this morning I read some reviews. The ones from 2017 and 2018 were good. The ones from 2024 were not. They were awful, and most complained about the same things. Erratic oven temps and difficulty adjusting the burners were the two main issues. No flame low enough for simmering . . . medium and high were the same . . . etc. Also, cleaning the top of the stove, which one reviewer described as a \"nightmare.\" Another said the cast-iron grates on top were linked together so both had to be removed at the same time, but I hope she was wrong about that. title: How are the community colleges in your area? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "elmerjfudd", "author_name": "Elmer J Fudd", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/elmerjfudd", "date": "2025-01-20", "text": "In my state, they don't seem to be very good. But I'm not sure exactly what goals and missions they work toward for students. Many do have important vocational programs - training and education in building trades, for becoming paraprofessionals in professional areas (medical and dental assistants, paralegals), other two year programs for study in areas such as fire and police public services. I'd always thought that another important service was to provide entry funnels for students desiring college study but with inadequate preparation out of high school. Such kids can use community colleges to raise their skills and knowledge in whatever academic fields interest them and prepare for transfer after two years to 4 year institutions. Also, as an adjunct, for students from lower socio-economic circumstances, community colleges offer inexpensive (and in some places, free) ways to complete the first two years of study toward bachelor's degrees. Also, there's some effort to provide classes of interest in the adult education area, for people interested in various topics but without matriculation or career directed intentions I was shocked to learn recently that transfer rates to four-year colleges are less than 20% overall in my state and for some community college, that number is in single digits. What the heck are they doing? Do the public funds spent for community college systems provide value for money or is it wasted to a greater extent than people realize? What can or should be done? If young people who attend community colleges don't ultimately transfer to 4 year colleges and don't complete the mostly 2 year vocational training programs that are offered, what's next for them in their lives? Are these the young 20-somethings and also older adults so often encountered working in restaurants or in retail with jobs paying at or near the minimum wage?", "images": []}

title: Common Exercises with a Dip Station Home Gym | Houzz Forum

It\u2019s a versatile and compact piece of equipment that allows for various upper-body exercises in a home workout setting. Benefits of a Dip Station Home Gym Upper Body Strength: Dips effectively work the triceps, pectorals, and deltoids, making them an excellent choice for developing upper body strength. Muscle Building: Dips are a great way to build muscle in the upper body, especially for the triceps and chest. By adjusting your body position or adding extra weight, you can progressively overload the muscles for growth. Core Engagement: While performing dips, your core is engaged to stabilize your body, making dips also a good exercise for strengthening the abdominal muscles. Improved Joint Health: When done correctly, dips can improve shoulder and elbow joint mobility, providing functional strength that benefits overall movement and posture. Space-Efficient: Dip stations home gyms are often compact and take up little space, making them ideal for home gyms with limited room. Versatility: Aside from traditional dips, dip stations can be used for other exercises like push-ups, leg raises, knee raises, muscle-ups, and straight-arm dips. Features to Look for in a Dip Station Home Gym Stability and Durability: The dip station home gym should be made of sturdy materials (like heavy-duty steel) to ensure it supports your body weight safely during exercises. Look for reinforced frames and wide, stable bases to prevent wobbling during dips. Adjustable Height: Some dip stations home gym come with adjustable height settings for the handles. This allows you to tailor the dip station to your body size and the type of dip you want to perform (e.g., wide-grip dips or narrow-grip dips). THANK YOU", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d6e22eb4078f937d_2653-w500-h414-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/413238af078f937e_2654-w500-h491-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ebb214eb078f937f_2656-w500-h280-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c28223ad078f9380_2657-w500-h288-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~2016304563", "author_name": "CHRISTINE HALL ARCHITECTS LTD", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~2016304563", "date": "2025-01-22", "text": "Hi there, I agree with everything everyone has already posted for you and have a couple of points to add. Firstly, if you are unhappy with the architect's first proposal for you, given they were provided all the information, including your budget, don't be afraid to switch architects. It would be hard to have a great relationship moving forward with the original architect. Secondly, make sure your budget is realistic for what you want. Having a more 'compact' plan may be what the architect thought would fit your budget. You wanted a 'creative, ambitious, bold and eye catching' design. Does your budget extend to the out of the ordinary solution you desire? Check out my website with the Hubbard house and Queenstown Home 03. Both of these have irregular plans and curved membrane roofs and are focused on the amazing view. The knock on effects of this are endless and the budget needs to accommodate these 'out of the box' ideas.  However, both of these have the views in the oposite direction to the sun so the 'warm roofs' were a good solution. Having said that, I agree that your proposed plan doesn't appear to capture your desires or the opportunities the site and views offer. PDS Design offers some lovely insight and I would suggest you definately look at engaging someone to come up with a new design after discussing all the issues with you, i.e, your breif, planning restrictions, budget etc. I am retiring so am not putting my name in the hat but you could ask one or two companies to offer concepts for you that should then both be priced before you proceed with a chosen one. A couple of design points - definitely agree that you should avoid internal gutters where possible. NZ is a high rainfall country so keeping water out of buildings is a high priority here. Things like corridor links, that have been suggested can have flatish roofs at lower levels to the main roofs but need to be really well detailed and correctly installed. Do you need 4 full bathrooms for a home of around 280-300 sq. m's? I would suggest some money could be saved by a better layout and possibly sharing a bathroom, unless that was your request originally. I would try, as has been suggested, to work with the slope to gain height with living spaces etc. What about having a garage and parking at the lower level with an entry and then create a terrace on top of that for the living and possibly bedroom/s to open onto. Given you have high rainfall, this should perhaps be covered or partly so, for you to use it or at least to have lounge doors open whilst there is light drizzle. What about an 'L' shaped plan with the court or terrace filling the space in the 'L' creating two 'wings' and the garage below. You don't have to be 'full frontal' to the view with a rectangular box and with careful window placement, you can maximise the view opportunities from almost every room. Big corner windows at the ends of the L can provide varying views. You can achieve a similar effect with two rectangular wings angling out from each other with a link towards the rear where they come closer. That will create a nice courtyard at the front and a smaller one at the back. One wing would be for living and the other for sleeping. The master would be at the end towards the view and the living would be arranged with the living at the view end, then the dining and the kitchen behind. The kitchen runnig accross the wing would have great views from the work bench/island. I could go on, but find someone else that you jell with to create your home. Don't be afraid to 'interview' a few before you choose the right team. Good luck, C.", "images": []}}

title: Own or rent in retirement? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "toronto-veterinarian", "author_name": "Toronto Veterinarian", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/toronto-veterinarian", "date": "2025-01-23", "text": "I was having a discussion with a friend today, and I thought I'd float it for comments:  What do you think about the pros and cons of renting or owning your home in retirement.  The type of home (house vs apartment) isn't an issue - my question is whether to own or rent. I am leaning towards renting, in part because I don't have children that could benefit from inheriting it.  Still, how many grown children (of parents who die in their 70s+) actually need or want their parents' house - wouldn't it just be sold and the profit distributed anyway?  I see no value in holding several hundreds of thousands of dollars in property, when that money could be used for whatever I want - not just living expenses, but maybe travel, hiring help, or equipment for hobbies.   I would spend as my budget would allow, and when I pass there would be no dwelling for my executor to manage. I'm in a house now, but I imagine in 5-7 years I'll be unable to manage it and will move somewhere smaller, which is how I came to be thinking about the rent vs. own issue.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "trainee", "author_name": "KW PNW Z8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/trainee", "date": "2025-01-23", "text": "My first thought is that where & how to live in retirement is a decision that should be reevaluated before retirement, at retirement & during retirement. It\u2019s not a once & done decision - it changes as health, needs, wants change. It\u2019s a very good thing to be thinking about retirement living well ahead of time & also a good thing to be talking to others about plans & ideas for it. It\u2019s a good way to hear other ideas to consider.  We (DH & I)talked a lot about what lifestyle we envisioned in retirement. We couldn\u2019t imagine renting because to us owning our home, mortgage free, represents more stability, privacy, control & choice. We did downsize to a smaller home & to a single story that was built with aging in place in mind. It has wider than standard hallways & doorways for walker & wheelchair accessibility & a flat yard. The floorplan supports having a live in caretaker or help with bed & bath privacy if that is ever needed. When we\u2019re unable to do the maintenance home ownership requires, or even now when we don\u2019t want to do it, we have the resources to pay someone to do it.  Our larger decision was deciding what city to live in. We knew we wanted to move away from our too busy & high traffic area to a place that still had easy access to an airport & to medical. We explored many places over 10 years preretirement to find our current home.  As I see it, our next decision point on where to live - whether to stay in the home we own or move into a retirement community will be health or death related. Would either of us want to stay in in this house alone? Would we both want to stay if neither of us could drive? What if one of us needs full time care due to either physical or cognitive decline?  The sale of our home would generate enough cash to facilitate an easier decision where the next home would be & our other resources are such that we could have caretaker help in this house if needed.", "images": []}}

title: Please help me remove this Herbeau faucet part so I can replace. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "tiffew", "author_name": "tiffew", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tiffew", "date": "2025-01-23", "text": "I have an 11 year old copper and brass Herbeau Flamande faucet in my kitchen. It, and the sprayer, are leaking. The sprayer leaks whenever the faucet is on ans this is the main concern. Herbeau said I need to replace the cartridge, but I cannot remove the cartridge housing, no matter how hard we try. They told us to squirt a water/vinegar combo into the seam to loosen anythjng that has hardened. We did that for over a day. I have tried WD40, various wrenches, rubber grips, etc. It wont budge. The brass is soft and the counter is marble, so we are also needing to be mindful of that. I\u2019m enclosing some photos for reference.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/02e200b407927012_0199-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jyl-gw", "author_name": "John Liu", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jyl-gw", "date": "2025-02-27", "text": "Tape some thick cardboard down on  the  marble  countertop  around  the  faucet,  then some plastic sheet.  You want  to  protect  the  marble  from  impact and  from  the  penetrating oil.  Add a folded bath towel as extra protection when the hammer comes out (below). Apply Kroil or PB Blaster, another penetrating oil  product.  Plenty of it.   Wait a day, reapply, wait a day. Get  the  correct six point closed end wrench.  It needs to be exactly  the  right size to fit on  the  hex surfaces - too large and you will round off  the  part.   This  will be a large wrench,  not  a common size. You  can  sometimes  rent tools  from  auto parts stores.  Set  the  adjustable wrench  to  fit  the  hex surface, tape  the  wrench jaw so it doesn\u2019t move,  bring that  wrench  to the  store  and  ask  for  a six point wrench of  that  size. While there, get a small tube of \u201canti-seize\u201d and a small brass wire brush.  I assume  you  have  brass and  copper polish, if  not  then  get  some. Place  the  closed end of the wrench on  the  part, pressed all  the  way onto  the  hex surfaces, wrench handle  more or less vertical.  Again,  the wrench must fit with  minimal play; if you  got the  wrong size, stop and  get the  right  size. Have someone  hold the  head of  the  wrench  firmly   onto  the  part  so it  doesn\u2019t slip.  Take a large hammer and strike  the  wrench handle, at  the  far end.  Start with little taps as practice controlling the hammer, then  hit moderately hard.  You are trying to use impact to break the thin corrosion  layer that is holding the part stuck.  The shock of impact  works better than  a steady pull.  After  the  part starts moving, use  the  wrench in  the  normal manner. The  protection  on the  marble  counter  is  there  if  you  drop  the  hammer etc.  The wrench is vertical so you aren\u2019t swinging  the  hammer down at  the  counter.  Be  very careful  all  the  same. After  you  get the  part off, and  have replaced  the  cartridge, use  the  polish  and a cloth  to  clean up  the  part  and the  rest of  the  faucet.  Really  polish  it up well.  The  hex surfaces may be marred a bit (brass is a crappy material  for  a hex nut), but  when  polished  shiny it   won\u2019t show (much). Use  the  wire brush  to  clean up  the  threads.  Apply anti-seize  to the  threads. Reinstall  the  part,  using  only  your  fingers to  turn it until the  threads engage (because you  do not want to  use the  wrench until  you are sure you  haven\u2019t cross-threaded the part) and  tighten it only  just  enough  to  not leak,  then  a tiny bit more. Be gentle: with  that  big wrench you or  more  likely  some ham-handed male helper can easily cross-thread the part or strip  the  threads. This is  how  you\u2019d break free then reinstall a large stuck nut on a car - e.g. an axle nut.  Well, on  the  car  you  might  use heat  to  break  the  corrosion,  and  you\u2019d torque  the  heck out of  the  nut  when  reinstalling.   But  you\u2019d clean  the  threads and  use  anti-seize,  so that the  next time  isn\u2019t  such  a  nightmare.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "bunty-pfvwus-pf~1479123723", "author_name": "Bunty", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/bunty-pfvwus-pf~1479123723", "date": "2025-01-24", "text": "We recently installed an HVAC system in our house, which is 3,200 sq. ft. with 12 ft. ceilings. The contractor installed a 5-ton system, but I\u2019m wondering if there\u2019s a way to confirm if this is appropriately sized for our home. Is there a calculation or method I can use to double-check this? Any insights or suggestions would be greatly appreciated. Thanks!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "author_name": "Charles Ross Homes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "date": "2025-01-24", "text": "\"A properly sized HVAC system is over sized upwards of 80-90% of the time as the outdoor temperature you live in constantly changes.\"  A properly-sized HVAC system is designed for a particular cooling load and a particular heating load at a particular set of summer and winter design temperatures, respectively.  The design temperatures are specified in the code for your area.  How often the system operates close to the design conditions depends on your climate.  If a properly-sized system is operating far from maximum or minimum design temperatures, it's not over-sized, it's simply operating far from the maximum or minimum design conditions.  For single-stage and single-speed systems, operating far from max/min design conditions typically results in reduced efficiency and may decrease occupant comfort as well.   More sophisticated (and expensive) systems (e.g., multi-stage, variable speed systems) provide better control, efficiency, and comfort over the full range of design conditions.", "images": []}}

title: Property development dilemma | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-797725834", "author_name": "HU-797725834", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-797725834", "date": "2025-01-24", "text": "Hi there, New to the forum and am keen to see if anyone is able to give some advice/insight on our property conundrum. We are in the very fortunate position to have recently purchased part of a farm. We are in our late 20\u2019s and the mortgage is pretty large. I am employed and my partner is self employed (builder) with a good income. We can afford the mortgage fairly comfortably currently, but could get pushed out of our comfort zone should interests go up too much more. The property consists of an old farm workers bungalow which we are currently living in but needs extension and full renovation. On the property we also have a large barn which with planning could be converted into a large home (at a guess would be worth \u00a3900,00 - 1,250,000 competed) The property is mortgaged as one property currently. We would love to extend and renovate the bungalow to live in with a view to maybe develop the barn in the future and rent as an income. In order to afford to do this we would need to remortgage within a couple of years to hopefully release enough funds to at least complete a large chunk of the build. However it also seems silly to have another barn sat empty for potentially years when it could be developed and potentially provide a rental income and equity to put towards developing the bungalow? Does anyone know how it would work in terms of getting a loan to renovate the barn, to then refinance it to cover costs of the build and potentially more to put towards renovating the bungalow? Could this then be technically deemed a separate property and have its own mortgage? We need to speak to a financial advisor really and will do at some point but we are just trying to get our head around the best plan and how to move forward. We would like to get married and have children in the next 3-4 years also so we would love to have the bungalow renovated before then, but also would like to make decisions that will give us more financial stability for the future. Any thoughts or ideas of what you would do?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-462192744", "author_name": "Isla Cherry", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-462192744", "date": "2025-01-30", "text": "You will have to sub-divide the land for starters. title: DAYLILY SEED QUESTION | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "alameda-gw", "author_name": "alameda/zone 8/East Texas", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/alameda-gw", "date": "2025-01-25", "text": "I harvested alot of daylily seeds last year - at first, got them put away in the refrigerator for growing later. Most are still floating - a good many have gone to the bottom and look plumped up and fat, but I see no radicles peeping out. Am I wasting my time with these seeds?  Are the floating ones no good?  Will the ones on the bottom have a chance of germinating?  I have quite a few other seeds in cups that didnt get refrigerated.  Any chance these could germinate and if so.......does anyone have suggestions on how I should go about it?  Thanks for any suggestions......... Judith", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "outpaientzero", "author_name": "outpaientzero", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/outpaientzero", "date": "2025-01-25", "text": "I've never dealt with Day lily seeds and always divided them to get more so don't take this to the bank so here it goes.I've never soaked seeds over 24 hrs and either put them is soil or put them in a damp paper towel.  Seeds need oxygen to germinate.  The oxygen causes cellular respiration that breaks down stored nutrients to make energy to grow.  Soaking speeds up bringing the seeds out of dormancy and softens the shell but you shouldn't over do the soaking time.I can't see how day lily seeds would be different from other seeds, but I really don't  believe three weeks sitting in stale anaerobic water they have any chance of growing. When I am ready to plant them, I pour a little water (I use distilled, but I don't know if that is necessary) in the baggie and put them back in the refrigerator. title: What's the problem with starting seeds early? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rick7072", "author_name": "Rick (zone 6b, MA)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rick7072", "date": "2025-01-26", "text": "I have a packet of snapdragon seeds where it's recommended that I start the seeds inside \"6-8 weeks before average last frost.\" I want to and will respect that recommendation, but out of curiousity: what is the problem with starting them earlier, assuming I have them in an appropriately-sized pot? Is it simply that before the weather is warm enough for planting, my plants may be quite large and I may run out of vertical and horizontal space on my grow light shelves?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "suzy-jackson88", "author_name": "suzy jackson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/suzy-jackson88", "date": "2025-02-01", "text": "I grow them when I have them. tbh...but since they tend to be mostly hardy herbaceous perennials/trees or shrubs, and I grow them either outdoors, in coldframes or the greenhouse, I am fairly blase about timing. As long as the soil isn't saturated, the seeds perform much as they would in a relatively natural setting. I tend not to use lights/heat unless I was attempting to adjust the seasonal requirements - such as back when I grew a lot of bell peppers which prefer a longer growth season than is readily available in a British climate, so would artificially start them into growth much earlier than they would naturally germinate in a UK spring. title: Chin up question and self-plateau or limitation. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2025-01-27", "text": "I know men's muscle and body weight are distributed differently so this is not about numbers, but it is about possible preconceptions about your limitations. When the thread came up about being able to do a chin up I was not sure I could do one because I hadn't tried in many years and I had always used the weight-assist machine for pullups but I haven't gone to a gym that has one for some time. I also can't jump up to the chin up bar at my current gym because it is high, and I have to climb up the machine which I was self conscious about. So as I said, I decided to try it to see if I could do one, and I was able to do eight, and within a few days I was doing eleven on average. I can't go all the way up on #12 so 11 is my current real plateau. \"Elite\" category for my age is somewhere around 15 +, and  most people at any age are 0-1. \"Novice.\" But I wonder if this is because it's not an exercise even people who work out, usually do. --I didn't, and I have been working out about 33%  of my life, distributed over about 50% of my life. Covid and post Covid knocked out about four solid years of regular workouts for example. I would suggest that you start by trying to hang by your body weight, and that you may find that the problem is partly grip or hand strength. But if you go to a gym, you should be able to set the barbell on the Smith machine well within reach and \"hang\" on it by lifting your legs up so you are not falling off a chin up bar. The other thing I was limiting myself on was the 45-degree leg press. For a couple of years I did the seated leg press where you push more or less straight out and a little \"up\". Women can usually lift a lot of weight on this machine, it looks like--on both machines really. You can do more on the 45-degree than the straight out because of leverage, I guess. When I switched to the 45, I put it at about the same weight as I was doing on the seated press, which was about my body weight or a little more--and it felt like I was lifting by the 15th rep--it did not feel way too light or anything. Then I thought, I hold up most of my body weight just walking around, so am I getting enough from this machine? So I doubled the weight of the plates I put on it. And I could still do it. Remember that on a machine that you can try to do one, and if you can't, and you are careful, you can just stop, it's not like dropping a free weight of having something fall on you. Then I saw a woman who was relatively small, a little taller than me but pretty thin, with 3  45 lb. plates on each side --which is triple where I had just started recently, so 270 lb. of plates plus the weight of the platform/sled you push the weight on, which \"feels like\" maybe 45 lb. of resistance, I don't know, and it's not written on the machine like at my old gym. So 270 is very slightly over twice my body weight, + the platform. And I can do three sets of 12, and I am not at terminal effort because I don't want to hurt myself. And I have a weak leg from nerve damage. I looked up about weights you can lift with your legs and apparently it's more than people think.  Again your  other limitation may be your joints rather than your muscles. So the point is not about what I can lift, but about finding out what I could actually do, that I did not think that I could. So if you do exercise, I would suggest a little safe experimentation to determine your actual limits.", "images": []}

title: What I've Learned About Growing Roses in Gopher Territory | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ddinsb", "author_name": "DDinSB (Z10b Coastal CA)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ddinsb", "date": "2025-01-27", "text": "If you don't have to contend with gophers, feel free to skip. I would prefer to garden without dealing with gophers. Yes, I recognize they fill a valuable niche in the environment. They aerate soils and bring important things to surface. You can see a story online about researchers dropping a bunch of gophers in an area that had just had volcanic eruption, and how the plots with gophers did so much better recovering than plots without gophers. I just wish they weren't in my immediate environment. Here's what I've learned. 1) I have to protect the planting areas. I've tried gopher wire cages, two kinds. One is Digger's heavy duty wire basket, five gallon. The other is a more flexible kind that you can stretch. The gophers have chewed through those flexi ones to get to dahlia bulbs, rose roots, and veggies. Gophers have also chewed holes in the bottoms of ceramic pots, plastic/resin pots, and oak barrels if the pots are on the ground. They start with a drainage hole, I think, and then enlarge it. So I either have to plant something in a gopher wire cage/basket in the pot, or put a flattened cage under the pot. But that's not foolproof. On the barrel, they were able to shimmy between the cage and the bottom of the barrel (probably because of the wood supports on the bottom). So -- must use the gopher wire cage/basket. Five gallon size works well for my rose bushes. One gallon works well for most kinds of perennial flowers that I want to keep.  In my raised veggie boxes I put what's called hardware cloth -- sturdy metal with tiny holes so you get drainage, but stronger and smaller holes than aviary or chicken wire. I put that under the box, and so far nothing has chewed through that! I tried doing that in a bed area, but the gophers went overground to get into that bed. So -- if I want to protect it, I have to put it in a gopher wire cage, a pot that's protected, or a raised bed with the wire under it. 2) Drawbacks to growing roses in gopher wire cages. Ideally, you're supposed to leave a bit of the wire exposed on top so the gophers don't just pop down into the cage from above, which I've seen them do. But this makes it challenging to pull weeds. And most challenging of all is that if you get a sucker, which Dr. Huey tends to do, you can't really get the right angle to pull the sucker off. I just dug up one of my favorite roses, a Distant Drums, because I couldn't get the sucker torn off, and it just kept regrowing and was starting to hurt the bush. So once I had it up, I planned to get it out of the wire cage so I could take care of the sucker. But Dr. Huey is so vigorous, the roots had gone well beyond the cage and were huge, so there was no way to take the rose out of the basket without probably really hurting the rosebush. So I did my best with the sucker, replanted the bush in a big pot, and will wait and see what happens now. If it suckers again from that spot, I will cut the roots off, and then take care of the sucker spot, and then re-pot it. Thankfully, I've learned that Distant Drums grows easily from a cutting, grows quite well own-root, so I won't be without the rose. But it's a shame to dig up this otherwise healthy and vigorous rose. Which is the problem with growing Dr. Huey grafted roses in a gopher wire cage! Another drawback is I have to make a hole big enough to fit the 5 gallon cage. If I've got a big, healthy, rose bush in a 5 gallon container or a big healthy bare root, no problem. But if it's a smaller rose, then it doesn't like being in such a huge hole. I don't know why it is -- but gardeners can tell you it's better to step up plants (from 4\" to 1 gallon to larger) before just plopping a small plant in a huge hole or a huge pot. I've learned the hard way that plopping my one-gallon roses, esp. own-root, in a humongous hole causes some roses to languish, or just take YEARS to really reach their potential. I've learned, therefore, to be patient and keep re-potting them.  Two roses I didn't have to wait long on -- as their roots are SUPER vigorous and easily made the transitions quickly -- Eisvogel and Mill on the Floss. And Distant Drums has proved to be very good on own-roots. Some are better than others. Lilas is still a puny little rose, as is Abraham Darby. 3) Plant plants that gophers don't like. They don't like lavender or rosemary, most sages, etc. They cannot eat gopher purge / spurge / euphorbia at all (poisonous) or daffodils/narcissus. They usually avoid thyme and African blue basil -- though this year they ate a sage, my African blue basil, and other plants they usually avoid. I'm not sure if they were super hungry, or just ate it because it was in their way. And one year I planted hundreds of daffodils thinking I'd create a barrier they would not cross, but they pushed out most of the daffodils so they dried up on top of the ground, I hadn't been walking around that area for a while, so didn't notice until it was too late. Cheeky little devils. 4) Despite all my efforts, I still get gophers in my beds, where they will eat things that are protected by cages if there are tasty bits low to the ground outside of the cages (like a dahlia that had several branches going out horizontally before going up). So then I try to kill them. I don't want to use poisons, as I don't want to poison something that might eat the gopher, so I use a variety of traps. The black box traps can work well, but you have to dig up a lot to get the durned thing in position. The gopher hawks worked like a charm for the first 3 years, but this last year I'm not having much luck. I think we've selected for the smarter gophers...and there is the trusty old McAfee trap which I onetime got my thumb in (ouch!), but is not working to get the one gopher in my garden right now. I've tried three different kinds of smoke bumbs. Not only do I feel like Wile E. Coyote using them, but I'm afraid I'll burn down my neighborhood. Nevertheless, I've not seen any effect, except that I think I may have killed a mole, which I feel terrible about. I saw the gopher while I was looking out my window, and he ws just taking deep breaths. So I think he was able to close off the tunnel with the gas, then just came up later, and went right back to chewing everything up. Someone recently suggested I rub the traps with onion, as supposedly this is what they do at Lotus Land (a garden nearby). I've also used gloves so my own smell is not on the traps. I think the crows are getting impatient. I usually put any dead gophers out on a big rock so they can come and have a feast. Nothing for a while. BTW -- if you use the gopher hawk, be sure to learn how to use it properly. You can wreck it if you don't do it right. I know, as even though I showed my husband and told him to watch the video online and sent him the link, when I got back from my travels last year I had to replace all the little wire parts -- which were $5.99 each. Plus tax. p.s. yes, I've seen Chunk the Groundhog videos. My problem with the ground squirrels and the gophers is that they eat the entire plant (squirrels from the top, gophers from below), so NO ONE gets any vegetables or flowers. I would share a carrot or green bean or rose with them -- but if they destroy the whole plant or the entire root system -- no one wins. Not even them! I DO feel bad killing them. Honestly. I cried the first few times. My husband told me to toughen up. My dad told me to cook it, and maybe I'd feel better about it, to which I replied, \"I'm not Granny from the Beverly Hillbillies!\" I think that's what I've learned. Yes, my life is like Caddyshack (the Chevy Chase film). Though I haven't tried blowing the gopher up. Yet. If you've learned something I should know, please enlighten me. If you have a trick, please share. And if you are just now encountering gophers -- I send you my deepest condolences and hope you find something here useful. If you live in an area that doesn't get gophers -- here's a video: https://www.dailymotion.com/video/x8hde4a or, if you don't care for the Hillbilly Bears and want live action: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/VVBEUvbbNX0 And here's an image/post/advice on salvaging roses from this forum: https://www.gardenweb.com/discussions/6245707/spring-rose-disaster", "images": []}

title: Another stump removal post: questions | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "central-valley", "author_name": "central_valley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/central-valley", "date": "2025-01-28", "text": "This is probably the 10,000th post on the topic, but I can't find answers in the ones I read. I started by getting out my old plastic can of Stump Out granules. They appear to be in good condition, but moisture and humidity have made the label unreadable. And the instructions are on the label. I searched the web but couldn't find them. After all, why should anyone put them on the web when they're right on the label...? I found some YouTube videos that told me what to do, but I also found references to something that's apparently in the instructions, that I never saw it before: that I'm supposed to \"season\" the stump for 18 months before I try to remove it. How is that supposed to work? This was an acacia tree. If I leave the stump for 18 months, I won't have a seasoned stump; I'll have a new tree. But onward. I found a 1\" augur bit which I don't remember buying, but I must have gotten it just for this purpose, because it did a great job of drilling into the tree. The augur just pulled the bit in... until the drill stalled, and I found that the bit was too firmly jammed to move when I reversed the drill. I had to take the the drill off and use a pipe wrench to remove the bit. Is there something I don't know here... a way to use an augur bit without having that happen? Finally, a question that has plagued me since the first time I drilled a stump. I'm supposed to drill 1\" vertical holes 10\" deep, but trees rarely grow straight down even if they grow straight up (which this one didn't). When I drill a hole that deep, I usually drill right through the base of the tree into soil. Then any water I pour into the hole just drains away. How can I tell where, and in what roughly vertical direction, it's safe to drill?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bill-mn_z3b", "author_name": "BillMN-z4a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bill-mn_z3b", "date": "2025-01-28", "text": "I tend to cut them as level with the ground as I can without getting my chain saw into the dirt, which can dull the chain and ruin the bar Muchos pronto. Maybe leave an inch or two above the ground to be safe. Additionally, you can burn out a stump, depending how large it is and if no burning regulations in place, by setting a metal 55-gal drum, with the bottom cut out, over it. First start a small charcoal fire on top of the stump, like you would for a charcoal grill. Then set the barrel on and dump a bag or two of charcoal in the barrel on top of the fire. It might burn for days and if it doesn't completely burn the stump, you can add charcoal and rinse/repeat. Some people use hardwood and just keep adding wood on top as it burns down. Within a day or two, the hot embers at the base of the fire will dry the stump out so it burns to ashes. Existing vegetation will no longer exist in that spot. Either way, it's going to be some work. title: I could hardly believe it! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "laceyvail", "author_name": "laceyvail 6A, WV", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/laceyvail", "date": "2025-01-28", "text": "As climate got warmer and warmer here, I began to be able to easily store savoy cabbages and winter lettuces in the garden.  The cabbages were just wrapped in 2 layers of row covers and the lettuces were under a little plastic tent, like a mini hoop house, and I harvested all winter.  Twice I had to use extraordinary protection when dips around zero for a night or two were predicted in a polar vortex.  This involved packing hay over the row covers and covering that with plastic for the cabbages and putting several layers of row covers over the lettuces but under the plastic and then packing hay over the row covers.  Both times the veggies came through perfectly. But this January, I had to do the same for over three weeks while we had the kind of cold we hadn't had in at least 10 years, nights in the single digits and days in the very low teens.  For part of that time there was some snow cover too, but the coldest nights--zero and just below--came after the snow cover was mostly gone.  When I finally was able to get a look at the veggies I was astonished to see that they were in pretty good shape.  The cabbages look quite good--some damage to outer leaves--and the lettuces needed a little cleaning up of dead, limp leaves but they'll regrow fast. I'm thrilled.  And completely astonished.", "images": []}
